We who are homeless.- Among Europeans today there is no lack of those who are entitled to call themselves homeless in a distinctive and honorable sense: it is to them that I especially commend my secret wisdom and gaya scienza. For their fate is hard, their hopes are uncertain; it is quite a feat to devise some comfort for them - but what avail? We children of the future, how could we be at home in this today? We feel disfavor for all ideals that might lead one to feel at home even in this fragile, broken time of transition; as for its "realities," we do not believe that they will last. The ice that still supports people today has become very thin; the wind that brings the thaw is blowing; we ourselves who are homeless constitute a force that breaks open ice and other all too thin "realities."

We "conserve" nothing; neither do we want to return to any past periods; we are not by any means "liberal"; we do not work for "progress"; we do not need to plug up our ears against the sirens who in the market place sing of the future: their song about "equal rights," "a free society," "no more masters and no servants" has no allure for us. We simply do not consider it desirable that a realm of justice and concord should be established on earth (because it would certainly be the realm of the deepest leveling and chinoiserie); we are delighted with all who love, as we do, danger, war, and adventures, who refuse to compromise, to be captured, reconciled, and castrated; we count ourselves among conquerors; we think about the necessity for new orders, also for a new slavery - for every strengthening and enhancement of the human type also involves a new kind of enslavement. Is it not clear that with all this we are bound to feel ill at ease in an age that likes to claim the distinction of being the most humane, the mildest, and the most righteous age that the sun has ever seen? It is bad enough that precisely when we hear these beautiful words we have the ugliest suspicions. What we find in them is merely an expression - and a masquerade - of a profound weakening, of weariness, of old age, of declining energies. What can it matter to us what tinsel the sick may use to cover up their weakness? Let them parade it as their virtue; after all, there is no doubt that weakness makes one mild, oh so mild, so righteous, so inoffensive, so "humane"!

The "religion of pity" to which one would like to convert us - oh, we know the hysterical little males and females well enough who today need precisely this religion as a veil and make-up. We are no humanitarians; we should never dare to permit ourselves to speak of our "love of humanity"; our kind is not actor enough for that. Or not Saint-Simonist enough, not French enough. One really has to be afflicted with a Gallic excess of erotic irritability and enamored impatience to approach in all honesty the whole of humanity with one's lust!

Humanity! Has there ever been a more hideous old woman among all old women - (unless it were "truth": a question for philosophers)? No, we do not love humanity; but on the other hand we are not nearly "Gerrnan" enough, in the sense in which the word "German" is constantly being used nowadays, to advocate nationalism and race hatred and to be able to take pleasure in the national scabies of the heart and blood poisoning that now leads the nations of Europe to delimit and barricade themselves against each other as if it were a matter of quarantine. For that we are too openminded, too malicious, too spoiled, also too well informed, too "traveled": we far prefer to live on mountains, apart, "untimely," in past or future centuries, merely in order to keep ourselves from experiencing the silent rage to which we know we should be condemned as eyewitnesses of politics that are desolating the Gennan spirit by making it vain and that is, moreover, petty politics: to keep its own creation from immediately falling apart again, is it not finding it necessary to plant it between two deadly hatreds? must it not desire the eternalization of the European system of a lot of petty states?

We who are homeless are too manifold and mixed racially and in our descent, being "modern men," and consequently do not feel tempted to participate in the mendacious racial self-admiration and racial indecency that parades in Germany today as a sign of a German way of thinking and that is doubly false and obscene among the people of the "historical sense." We are, in one word - and let this be our word of honor - good Europeans, the heirs of Europe, the rich, oversupplied, but also overly obligated heirs of thousands of years of European spirit. As such, we have also outgrown Christianity and are averse to it - precisely because we have grown out of it, because our ancestors were Christians who in their Christianity were uncompromisingly upright: for their faith they willingly sacrificed possessions and position, blood and fatherland. We - do the same. For what? For our unbelief? For every kind of unbelief? No, you know better than that, friends! The hidden Yes in you is stronger than all Nos and Maybes that afflict you and your age like a disease; and when you have to embark on the sea, you emigrants, you, too, are compelled to this by - a faith!

- Friedrich Nietzsche,

“If you are depressed you are living in the past. If you are anxious you are living in the future. If you are at peace you are living in the present.”

― Lao Tzu

While looking at an unbroken string, the mental act of breaking it into a start, middle, and end is purely inventive and has no bearing on the string, yet it is our perception that makes such distinctions meaningful. Time in this sense is like a string; it is an unbroken phenomenon that we break apart piecemeal, and given our conceptual and biological limits, we cannot do otherwise.

Within the context of mental deliberation, it is useful to break apart a past, present, and future tense of the deliberative instinct. What I mean by deliberative instinct in this sense is the temporal inclination between past, present, and future in the act of considering the means to an end. In this case specifically, the end is one's personal vital trajectory, and the means are the individual decisions and minor actions we make in the process of our individual becoming. It must be remembered that consciousness is always consciousness of something, and this intentionality of thought betrays the content of our character.

In much of the ancient world, man had a very lopsided way of thinking, and this was in the form of reverence for past figures. Various gods, beasts, men, heroes, and villains of the past lived on in the minds of the men of antiquity in the way they lived, in their personal deliberations, and in their ambitions for the future. The vital trajectory of a man was always juxtaposed in the context of his history. This is plain from much of the customs of the ancients. How many wildly different peoples used naming conventions such as "Z, son of Y, son of X", or "X of [insert city of origin]"? This naming convention crops up among peoples as different as the ancient Hebrews in the Old Testament, to the Teutons in the Saga of the Völsungs. Ancient Rome is an excellent example of this; Patrician families possessed rooms in their estates displaying the wax molds of the faces of that family's ancestors; young children would be shown these faces and told of their deeds, and it is said that this experience made young Roman children burn with the ambition to emulate and outdo their ancestors.

At some point in history, western man experienced a shift in his thinking. This destabilization of consideration can be traced to the doctrine of Christianity, which sullies one's ancestors by teaching a past full of sin, and a future of salvation and redemption. Instead of placing so much weight on deliberation of the past, and the desire to live up to one's ancestors, man became much more inventive in his ideas, perhaps to get closer to God. This way of thinking is anticipation of the future; it is anxiety, anticipation, and irritability. In short, thinking on the credit of potential is to live in the land of the not-yet.

In the modern world of the 21st century, I see a large shift away from both of these instincts of deliberation. People are either completely uninitiated with their history, or jaded by it, fully convinced that we've made "progress" instead of mere process. At the same time, the future is taken for granted among Christian, Socialist, and Transhumanist alike. The modern Christian has lost much of the severity of past Christians, and thus their doctrine has degraded - a trend since Martin Luther at least. The modern Christian rests content believing that they are heaven-bound. Socialists are nearly identical to Christians in form, though not content; their hopeless dream of revolution is an ugly transliteration of the Christian apocalypse - merely replace the destruction of "sin" with "bourgeois". Transhumanists meanwhile, are similarly shallow, believing vainly in the eschatological "singularity", wherein their hedonism can be gratified for all eternity.

In all these cases, the succor for the "not-yet" dulls; for even though they still have future-bound ideas, these ideas are not ambitions, these are bits of imagination trapped permanently in the future, and cannot be attained. When something is trapped in forever outside the horizon, it's safe to declare it alien to the system, and however you justify it metaphysically, these ideas are the ultimate non-thing in the course of our destiny - eschatology to put it simply. Heaven is not an idea that one is allowed to work for, as it is a gift. The Revolution according to Marx was a mechanical inevitability, yet this wistfulness is nothing more than complacency, and the future of Utopian Socialism lies in a perpetual state of "just a little bit longer". The singularity too, falls under this general theme; technology is a wonderful thing, but is an empty form that requires human effort to give it meaning.

When one puts no stock in history, and puts faith into an abstraction that cannot be worked for, then one comes to the realization that nothing can be the subject of serious deliberation, which is to say, there are no collective ends - on a grand scale, a people face a pressing nihilism. This is the state of affairs that the west has been in, starting in the Enlightenment, and fructifying the 20th century. We aren't inspired by our ancestors. We are unable to work towards our ideals, as no matter how inventive and pretty we make them out to be they are still immaterial phantasms. We are forced to live in the present. This is the time we have been thrown into. Such is our fate.

As dreary and depressing as the collective drift surely is, that doesn't leave select individuals without hope, or to phrase my proposition better: there are still vital avenues to direct your ambition. For although our civilization merely drifts, and although it is riddled with pitfalls to retard the development of the naturally excellent, it is still possible to develop oneself intellectually and physically; and in fact, the world of today offers unparalleled means for the betterment of the individual who will try.
A meditation on time and deliberation...
